title: Hong Kong Milk Tea
subtitle: Silky pulled milk tea brewed strong and finished with evaporated milk
excerpt: Hong Kong milk tea is deliberately brewed bitter-strong, then cut with cold evaporated milk for a silky, creamy finish unlike any other tea style. Pulling the tea between two jugs aerates it and smooths the texture. Serves 2.
sourceNotes: Hong Kong milk tea (gong cha) developed in Hong Kong cha chaan tengs (tea restaurants) during British colonial administration, blending the British tradition of strong tea with milk with the Cantonese preference for condensed or evaporated milk. By the mid-20th century the style -- brewed from a blend of Ceylon and Assam black teas, pulled through a fine filter to aerate, and served with evaporated milk -- had become a defining feature of Hong Kong cafe culture. UNESCO recognised cha chaan teng culture on Hong Kong's intangible cultural heritage list in 2014.

content.text: This makes 2 cups and takes about 15 minutes. The key is brewing the
black tea blend
far stronger than you would drink it on its own -- the bitterness is necessary, because the
evaporated milk
(not fresh milk, never fresh milk) softens and sweetens the brew into something rounded and almost silky.
Traditional Hong Kong tea masters use a cloth filter called a
silk stocking strainer
-- a fine fabric sock on a wire frame -- which both strains the tea and contributes to the smooth texture. A fine-mesh sieve works at home. More important is
pulling the tea
: pouring the strained tea from one jug to another from a height, repeatedly, to aerate it and lower the temperature slightly before adding milk.
What you need

items.prepNote: loose leaf, or 3 strong tea bags
loose leaf, or 1 strong tea bag

content.text: Method

Bring 500 ml of water to a full rolling boil in a saucepan. Add all the tea leaves (or bags) and simmer gently over medium-low heat for 5 minutes. The tea should brew to a very deep amber, close to mahogany. This is intentional.
Place a fine-mesh sieve over a heatproof jug. Pour the brewed tea through the sieve, pressing gently on the leaves to extract fully. Discard the leaves.

Pull the tea: from a height of about 30 cm above a second jug, pour the tea in a steady stream. Raise the first jug to its full extension as you pour. This aerates the tea and creates the characteristic slight froth. Pour back from the second jug to the first. Repeat three times.
Add sugar if using. Stir to dissolve while the tea is still hot.

Divide the evaporated milk between two cups -- about 40 ml each. Pour the hot pulled tea over the top. The milk will cloud and swirl through the tea. Do not stir -- the temperature differential creates the characteristic colour gradient. Serve immediately.
For iced milk tea (yuan yang style): pull the tea as above, cool for 10 minutes, pour over ice, and add the evaporated milk. Stir before drinking.

items.cause: Tea was steeped rather than simmered, or too little tea was used
items.fix: Simmer the tea in the water (do not just steep) for the full 5 minutes. Use a generous 10 g of Ceylon leaf -- Hong Kong milk tea is deliberately brewed to a concentration most Western drinkers would find undrinkable on its own.

items.cause: Tea was too hot when the milk went in, or the evaporated milk was near its use-by date
items.fix: Pull the tea 3-4 times to lower the temperature before adding milk. Use chilled evaporated milk from a freshly opened can.

items.cause: Fresh milk was used instead of evaporated milk
items.fix: Evaporated milk is essential. Its concentrated fat and protein content gives the characteristic body that fresh milk cannot replicate.

content.text: Where this dish lives

Hong Kong milk tea developed in cha chaan teng tea restaurants from the 1940s onwards. It blends British colonial tea habits with local taste. The silk stocking strainer gives the tea its Cantonese name. It is a drink specific to Hong Kong, different from British tea and from Taiwanese bubble tea.
